statement: A Windows desktop editor for Group Policy administrative-template settings, used by administrators and power users. It works on all Windows editions, including Home, which lack the built-in editor, and on offline user profiles, policy files and the live registry.

evidence.shows: States the goal: Group Policy editing for all Windows editions.
Opens the saved policy source or the local policy object at startup.

statement: It runs on the user's own Windows machine, as a 32- or 64-bit process on the .NET Framework 4.5.2 runtime, reading and writing that machine's registry and policy files. There is no server or network service.

evidence.shows: Windows executable targeting .NET Framework 4.5.2.
Runtime pinned to .NET Framework 4.5.2.
Requires .NET Framework 4.5.2 on Windows Vista or newer.

statement: A person launches the program, which opens the main window; closing that window ends it. On start it loads the saved policy definitions folder and policy sources from the user's registry, and on close it releases any mounted registry hives. Several copies may run at once.

evidence.shows: Main form is the start window; app shuts down when it closes.
Single-instance mode is off.
Closing the main window cleans up policy sources.

statement: Built with MSBuild on a GitHub-hosted Windows runner whenever master changes or on manual trigger; the Release executable is hashed and uploaded to an AWS storage bucket as the latest build. Git commit text is embedded as the version. Tagged releases are published by hand on GitHub; no test step exists.

evidence.shows: Runs on push to master or manual dispatch, on a Windows runner.
Embeds version, compiles Release, computes hash.
Uploads the executable to S3 as PolicyPlusLatest.exe.
Releases are published on the GitHub Releases page.

statement: Work begins only when a person uses the window: menu choices, double-clicking a policy, and dialog buttons raise form events. There are no command-line arguments, network listeners or other programs calling in. A first-run prompt may also start the ADMX download.

evidence.shows: Load event runs startup work; later work comes from menu events.
First-run prompt offers the ADMX download.
Menu click handler opens a dialog and reloads.

statement: One edit: the person opens a policy, the dialog changes its state in an in-memory copy of the policy source, then File | Save writes it. Saving writes the policy file or registry, updates the policy version file, and asks Windows to refresh policy (or copies the difference into the registry on Home editions). It reports success or failure in a message box.

evidence.shows: Save writes comments and sources, stores choices, shows result message.
Local policy save writes file, refreshes or applies difference to registry.
Per-user policy save refreshes policy.

statement: Nothing runs around every action. There is no sign-in, request pipeline or interceptor; the only common step is the operating system's own elevation prompt at launch, and a read-only or writable check when a policy source opens.

evidence.shows: Asks for highest available privilege at launch.
Reports each source's writability after opening.

statement: No scheduled or batch work exists. Everything runs when a person acts; the only background threads are the ADMX download and the policy search, each started by a button.

evidence.shows: Download runs on a background task started by a button.
Search runs on a background task when the results window opens.

statement: The program has no users or roles of its own; the operating system decides. It asks for the highest privilege the person has, and what it can change depends on that: policy folders and machine registry need an administrator. It tests writability and marks sources unmodifiable.

evidence.shows: Runs with highest available privilege.
Tests write access to the registry policy key.
Reports sources as modifiable, not saveable or read-only.

statement: Not applicable: it is a single-user desktop tool with no customers or organisations. It can edit another Windows user's policies only by loading that person's registry file or per-user policy folder by hand.

evidence.shows: Other users' policy folders or hive files are opened by explicit choice.

statement: The program keeps its few preferences (last definitions folder, last policy sources, first-run flag) in the current user's registry under a Policy Plus key, plus language choice. It holds no secrets and no configuration file beyond the runtime version pin. Build secrets are GitHub Actions secrets outside the code.

evidence.shows: Reads saved sources from the user's registry key.
Opens the settings key under the current-user registry.
Storage bucket and access keys come from GitHub secrets.

statement: Failures are shown to the person in message boxes and nothing is logged to a file or service; there are no retries. Some errors are deliberately swallowed: unreadable saved sources fall back to local defaults, a failed settings key means preferences are not kept, and a comment-file error is ignored.

evidence.shows: Message box, then default sources.
Registry key failure is ignored silently.
Comment save errors are ignored.
Download failure shows only the failed phase.

statement: The program targets .NET Framework 4.5.2, which Microsoft stopped supporting in April 2022, so the runtime this tool depends on no longer receives security fixes.

evidence.shows: Targets .NET Framework 4.5.2.
Runtime version pinned to 4.5.2.

statement: The ADMX download fetches a Microsoft installer over the network and unpacks it with no checksum or signature check, then, as administrator, takes ownership of and overwrites the Windows policy-definitions folder with its files.

evidence.shows: Downloads the MSI and runs msiexec on it without verification.
Takes ownership of the destination and moves files into it.

statement: The release workflow gives the AWS keys to a third-party upload action pinned only to a version tag, and uses an old checkout action; a compromised action could take the keys or alter the published executable.

evidence.shows: Third-party S3 upload action receives AWS access keys.
Old checkout action version tag.

statement: A person launches the program, which opens the main window; closing that window ends it. On start it loads the saved policy definitions folder and policy sources from the user's registry, and on close it releases any mounted registry hives.

evidence.shows: Windows executable started through the application framework.
Load event restores saved definitions and policy sources.
Closing the main window cleans up policy sources.

statement: Built with MSBuild from the Visual Studio project, with Debug and Release configurations; a batch script embeds the Git commit as the version before building. We cite no automated pipeline or release steps; there is no test project and no per-environment configuration.

evidence.shows: Debug and Release build configurations.
Writes the Git commit description into the version file.
Manual build steps in Visual Studio.

statement: Nothing runs around every action. There is no sign-in, request pipeline or interceptor; the only common step is a writable-or-read-only check made when each policy source opens.

evidence.shows: Reports each source's writability after opening.
Application manifest is attached to the project.

evidence.shows: Tests write access to the registry policy key.
Reports sources as modifiable, not saveable or read-only.
Checks whether the user is an administrator.

evidence.shows: Reads saved sources from the user's registry key.
Opens the settings key under the current-user registry.

statement: Errors are swallowed in places: if the settings key cannot be opened, preferences silently are not kept, and a failed comment save is ignored, so a person can lose notes without being told.

evidence.shows: Registry key failure is ignored silently.
Comment save errors are ignored.
